what_it_does: Exfoliating AHA that helps smooth skin texture and support clearer-looking pores.
summary_short: Mandelic acid is an alpha hydroxy acid used to exfoliate the skin surface. Its larger molecular size makes it slower-feeling than glycolic acid, so it is often chosen for sensitive or blemish-prone skin.
summary_long:
Mandelic acid is an alpha hydroxy acid (AHA). In skincare, AHAs help loosen the bonds between dead skin cells on the surface, supporting smoother texture, a brighter look, and more even tone over time.

Compared with smaller AHAs like glycolic acid, mandelic acid has a larger aromatic structure. In practical use, that often makes it feel gentler and slower-acting, which is why it appears in products aimed at sensitive, oily, or blemish-prone skin.

The PubMed abstracts provided here mostly discuss mandelic acid as a chemical building block, its microbial production, and bacterial degradation pathways—not direct human skincare trials. For example, reviews describe mandelic acid and derivatives as useful synthetic blocks and discuss enzymes involved in producing or breaking down mandelic acid [PMID:unknown]. This means the skincare-specific evidence in these sources is thin, so consumer expectations should be based on its general AHA role rather than strong clinical claims from these abstracts.

Like other exfoliating acids, mandelic acid can sting, dry, or irritate skin, especially when overused or layered with other strong actives. Start slowly, avoid using it on compromised skin, and use sunscreen during the day because exfoliation can make skin more sun-sensitive.

It commonly pairs well with moisturizers, barrier-supporting ingredients, and sunscreen. Be careful combining it in the same routine with retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, scrubs, or other acids unless the product is designed that way.
quick_facts: Often used for texture and dullness
Popular for sensitive or blemish-prone skin
Can sting or dry skin if overused
Avoid layering with many strong actives
